title: Bilateral Anterior and Intermediate Uveitis with Occlusive Vasculitis as Sole Manifestation of Relapse in Multiple Sclerosis
case_prompt:
A 76-year-old German Caucasian woman with a history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis in remission for more than 30 years, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, and heavy cigarette smoking presented with increased glare and a sudden decrease in visual acuity in both eyes over a few days. Her ophthalmic history included left-eye amblyopia, retrobulbar optic neuritis in the left eye in 1986 and in the right eye in 1987 (diagnosed as MS and treated with azathioprine), and bilateral cataract surgery with intraocular lens implantation in 2012. Six months before presentation, she experienced decreased vision in the right eye diagnosed elsewhere as anterior uveitis and vitreous hemorrhage, but she did not follow up.

On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was counting fingers in the right eye and 0.32 in the left eye without improvement with refraction. Intraocular pressures were 19 mmHg (right) and 22 mmHg (left). Slit-lamp examination of both eyes showed 3+ anterior chamber cells, granulomatous endothelial precipitates, vitreous turbidity with cells and snowballs, mild sheathing of retinal vessels, and adjacent retinal hemorrhages. In the left eye, there were posterior synechiae and precipitates on the IOL surface.

Macular optical coherence tomography in the right eye revealed inflammatory cells in the vitreous, an epiretinal membrane, preserved foveal architecture, and parafoveal thickening without cysts or detachment; the left eye showed inflammatory cells, an epiretinal membrane without traction, and preserved foveal architecture without cysts or detachment. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated in the right eye blockage of choroidal fluorescence from vitreous opacities, ischemic areas in the inferotemporal arcade, collateral vessel formation, and leakage near the optic nerve head and along retinal veins; the left eye showed similar blockage, macular leakage, and periphlebitis.

Neurologic examination was normal with intact cranial nerves, no motor deficits, no pyramidal signs, and normal reflexes. MRI of the orbits showed no optic neuritis, and brain MRI revealed no acute inflammatory lesions. Paraclinical testing showed: normal serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and unremarkable chest x-ray; negative ANA and ANCA; HbA1c 5.2%; no cardiac arrhythmias; negative serologies for syphilis, Bartonella, and Lyme disease; carotid Doppler without plaques, dissection, or stenosis; and vitreous biopsy from the right eye showing no malignant lymphocytes with negative PCR for Herpes simplex, Varicella Zoster, Cytomegalovirus, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Sarcoidosis considered and excluded — “Sarcoidosis was excluded by normal serum angiotensin converting enzyme, and there were no relevant abnormalities on chest x-ray.”  
2. Systemic autoimmune disease (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus) considered and excluded — “Other diseases possibly associated with ocular signs were not likely on absence of systemic clinical findings, negative ANA, and ANCA, normal HbA1c (5,2%), and no heart rhythm abnormalities.”  
3. Infectious causes (Syphilis, Bartonellosis, Lyme disease) considered and excluded — “Infectious etiologies such Syphilis, Bartonellosis, and Lyme disease were also ruled out.”  
4. Ischemic vascular causes considered and excluded — “Regarding ischemic causes, Carotid Doppler showed no plaques, dissection, or stenosis.”  
5. Ocular lymphoma (masquerade syndrome) considered and excluded — “the absence of malignant suspicious lymphocytes … in a vitreous sample from RE excluded ocular lymphoma (Masquerade syndrome)… PCR tests in that sample were negative for Herpes simplex, Varicella Zoster, Cytomegalovirus, and Mycobacterium Tuberculosis.”  
6. Multiple sclerosis relapse considered as the remaining cause — “given the exclusion of other possible etiologies, diagnosis was … attributable to a MS relapse.”
